book: A Life’s Work: On Becoming a Mother
author: Rachel Cusk
en_title: A Life’s Work: Reading an Old Poem Again
zh_deck: 母婴聚会里接错的一句话，读过却没有读懂的一首诗。卡斯克把初为人母的狼狈、幽默和偏见一起写下，也让文学重新进入照顾孩子的日子。
en_deck: An awkward conversation and a newly understood poem bring Cusk’s bewilderment, humor, and prejudices into a memoir of early motherhood.
genre_zh: 回忆录 · 文学与照顾

zh_title: 《成为母亲》：她怎样重新读懂了一首诗
zh_body:
卡斯克参加过一次母婴聚会。谈起在场一位母亲很会烤蛋糕，她终于找到可以接下去的话题，兴冲冲地问：做这个能赚钱吗？对方和旁边的人交换了一个惊讶的眼神。她又说错话了。

《成为母亲》有不少这样的尴尬。作者原本以为，既然大家都在养孩子，总会有些话可以说。可是，被安排在同一种生活里，并不意味着彼此就成了同一种人。她问收入，未必是有意贬低家中的劳动；她只是还习惯于从工作、职业和外部世界理解一件事。对话卡住的那一刻，读者也看见了这个习惯。

这本书写于她初为人母的几年间，以怀孕、生产和照顾幼女的经历为中心。卡斯克当时已经是小说家，她没有因此写得更从容，反而把自己的惊慌、刻薄和不知所措都带进了书里。她看别人，也毫不客气地看自己。读这本书，常会先觉得好笑，随后意识到，刚才使人发笑的处境其实相当难熬。

因此，它并非温和地替母亲们说几句公道话。它更像是一个原先相信自己能够安排生活的人，忽然发现，最亲密的关系正在改变“安排”这件事本身。她不能把孩子当作一天中新增的一项工作，做完之后就回去过原来的日子；可她也没有一夜之间成为一个只想带孩子的人。

## 会读书的人，为什么也不知道怎么办

生育把卡斯克带进了一个建议特别多的世界。饮食、哺乳、睡眠，件件都有说明；她面对的却是一个不会按说明作出反应的婴儿。书里谈到肠绞痛，也谈到哺乳的困难。她到哺乳门诊求助，写起一排哭闹的婴儿，用的是近乎沸腾的声响，而不是母婴宣传册里那种安宁。

这种落差构成了本书的喜剧感。建议往往条理分明，照顾却发生在睡眠不足、拿不准下一步的时候。问题并非知识没有用，而是读懂一段话和照顾好眼前这个孩子之间，还有很长一段路。原先赖以获得信心的本领，到了这里未必立即奏效。

她尤其擅长把这种不确定写得近乎荒诞。在她笔下，一件喂养小事可能带上秘密行动的紧张。夸张有时会使读者不耐烦：事情真的有这么严重吗？但这种语气也准确保留了初学者的处境。对熟手来说只是换一种办法，对她来说，却可能牵涉自己是不是正在害孩子、是不是已经失败。

卡斯克没有把这种狼狈全归给外界。她也写出了自己的控制欲：既然如此努力地学习和尝试，生活为什么仍不肯恢复秩序？婴儿当然无法替她回答。孩子哭闹，不是为了驳倒母亲的计划；可在疲惫的人那里，两者很容易被感受为同一件事。

这使《成为母亲》比一份关于育儿负担的清单多了一层。负担可以统计，内心的冲突却不那么整齐。人既想照顾好孩子，也想重新获得胜任感；两种愿望纠缠在一起，有时连自己都分不清，眼下着急的是孩子还没舒服，还是自己又没能把事情办好。

## 说“留在家里”的时候，究竟留下了什么

卡斯克在序言里交代，伴侣后来辞去工作照顾孩子，好让她写这本书。旁人不停追问他今后打算做什么，仿佛照顾孩子并不足以回答这个问题。他的回答则把两件事放到一起：他带孩子，她写关于带孩子的书。

这段近乎冷笑话的对话，点明了写作的实际条件。没有人接过孩子，作者就未必能把自己经历过的事写出来。一本谈母职的书，如果把腾出时间的那个人完全藏在背后，也就容易让写作看起来只是意志力的结果。

但这项调整并没有让卡斯克的矛盾立即消失。她在序言中谈到，离开孩子与留在孩子身边，各有各的困难。前者不是毫无牵挂的自由，后者也不是自然圆满的归属。工作与照顾怎样分配，必须谈；谈妥了，也未必能一并分配好人的感情。

由此再回头看母婴聚会里的蛋糕问题，就不只是作者不懂社交。她想在新的生活中找到旧世界的入口，别人却未必愿意从那个入口交谈。共同的母亲身份没有消除她们之间的差异，也没有替她准备好朋友。离开原来的职业环境以后，连随口接上一句话，都可能需要重新学习。

这里既有孤立，也有卡斯克自己的偏见。她观察那些母亲时相当尖锐，有时让人觉得，她并不特别愿意了解对方为何珍惜眼前的生活。读者不必替她把每一份不适都辩护成洞见。恰恰因为这是一个具体女人的自述，她的局促、优越感和求助之心才会同时出现。删掉其中不讨人喜欢的部分，书倒可能失去可信之处。

## 厨房之外，还有诗里的房间

在这部书中，文学并不是用来装饰育儿经验的名言。卡斯克会带着新的困惑，回到从前读过的作品。《午夜霜寒》便是其中尤其动人的一处。她重新注意到，柯勒律治那首诗里有一个婴儿，也有一个留在屋中陪着婴儿的大人。

诗作于十八世纪末。夜深了，旁人已经睡下，父亲坐在屋中，思绪从眼前的寂静飘回自己的童年。他曾被困在城市与学校的生活中，于是盼望身旁的孩子将来能在山水之间长大。屋里很静，诗却没有停在这间屋里；记忆、愿望和窗外的四季，都随着他的思绪进来了。

对于正觉得自己被困在家中的卡斯克，这首诗的力量便有了变化。她以前读过它，如今却从陪伴婴儿的处境里读到了别的东西：身体留在原处，并不意味着心智只能收缩。孩子使人牵挂，也使一个人开始想象自己不会亲历的未来。

这不是文学替现实开出的止痛药。诗读完了，婴儿仍需要照顾，夜里仍可能无法安睡。但它让卡斯克暂时摆脱了一个过于窄小的二选一：要么回到过去那个能自由写作的自己，要么只剩眼前的母亲身份。她正在经历的改变，也可以成为思想的来处，改变她读书、看世界的方式。

我们因此能够理解，为什么书里那些文学岔路并非全可删去。若只想知道母婴生活的实际情况，它们有时确实显得绕远；但对这个作者来说，阅读本来就是她理解经验的一种办法。《午夜霜寒》之所以在此刻有用，不在于它证明做母亲最终一定幸福，而在于它容纳了困守与舒展同时发生的可能。

介绍这本书，也不宜把这个时刻写成圆满的大结局。某一次阅读改变了她看待生活的角度，不等于以后所有委屈都迎刃而解。卡斯克留下来的，恰恰是这种不稳定：刚获得一点理解，下一场哭闹可能又把人推回混乱。

## 不必先把她变成一位可爱的母亲

《成为母亲》出版后引起过强烈争议。一部分读者认出了自己不敢明说的感受，另一部分读者则很难忍受她的怨怼和夸张。中文译者黄建树谈到这本书时，特意提醒读者，书中既有阴郁，也有温柔，不能只留下其中一种。

这个提醒比简单赞扬“敢说真话”更准确。真实并不等于只写最难堪的感受，也不等于每一个判断都正确。卡斯克的厉害之处，是不肯在一句话后面立刻补上一句保证，把刚刚出现的冲突抹平。她允许烦躁持续一阵，也允许温柔在并不体面的地方出现。

书的范围仍须看清。作者能够出版、能够与伴侣调整工作，并非没有资源的照顾者。她选择少写某些家庭成员和背景，也使读者不能把这份自述当成全家的完整记录。一个人的感觉很真，与她对所有人的描写都公允，是两件不同的事。

不过，这些限制不妨碍本书提出那个难以轻轻带过的问题：一个女人成了母亲以后，还能不能以一个有判断、会出错、并不总让人满意的人出现？如果只能赞美她的奉献，或者谴责她的自私，我们知道的仍然只是两种角色，未必更懂得这个人。

卡斯克做的，是把角色里面的生活写了出来。她有时候误解别人，有时候终于理解一首旧诗；她没有停止爱孩子，也没有停止惦念自己的工作。这本书不要求我们决定，哪个部分才算真正的她。它让我们看见，她还在这些彼此牵扯的愿望之间生活，也仍在寻找能把它们说清楚的句子。
en_body:
At a gathering for mothers and babies, Rachel Cusk hears about another mother’s skill at baking cakes. At last she sees a conversational opening and asks enthusiastically whether it makes money. The woman exchanges a surprised look with someone nearby. Cusk has said the wrong thing again.

A Life’s Work contains many such embarrassments. She had imagined that raising children would provide common ground. But being placed in similar circumstances does not make people the same. Asking about income need not mean deliberately disparaging domestic labor. She still habitually understands an activity through work, a profession, and the outside world. The stalled conversation makes that habit visible.

Written during her first years of motherhood, the book centers on pregnancy, birth, and caring for a young daughter. Being an established novelist did not make Cusk more composed. She brought her alarm, sharpness, and bewilderment into the writing. She scrutinizes other people and herself with little gentleness. We may first laugh, then realize how difficult the situation behind the laughter was.

This is more than a sympathetic defense of mothers. Someone who believed she could organize her life discovers that an intimate relationship is changing the meaning of organization itself. The child cannot be treated as one extra task, after which ordinary life resumes. But neither has Cusk suddenly become someone who wants only to care for a baby.

## Why knowing how to read does not mean knowing what to do

Childbirth brings Cusk into a world overflowing with advice. Feeding, diet, sleep: everything has instructions. The infant before her does not respond according to them. She writes about colic and difficulties with breastfeeding. When she seeks help at a clinic, her account of crying babies evokes something approaching a boil, rather than the tranquility of a maternity brochure.

The contrast supplies much of the book’s comedy. Advice arrives in orderly form; care takes place amid sleep deprivation and uncertainty. Knowledge is not useless, but understanding a paragraph and caring for this particular child are separated by considerable distance. The abilities on which she once based her confidence do not immediately work here.

She can make uncertainty seem almost absurd. An ordinary matter of feeding acquires the tension of a clandestine operation. The exaggeration may irritate readers: is it really so serious? Yet it preserves the novice’s experience. What an expert sees as a simple change of method may leave her wondering whether she is harming the child or has already failed.

Cusk does not blame everything on outside expectations. She also reveals her desire for control. After all this study and effort, why will life not return to order? The baby cannot answer. Crying is not an attempt to refute the mother’s plans, although exhaustion can make the two feel much the same.

This gives the book something an inventory of childcare burdens cannot capture. Burdens can be counted; internal conflicts are less orderly. Wanting to make the child comfortable becomes entangled with wanting to feel competent again. Sometimes even the parent cannot tell which is causing the immediate distress: the baby remains uncomfortable, or she has once again failed to get things right.

## What remains when someone stays at home?

In the introduction, Cusk explains that her partner left his job to care for the children so that she could write this book. People kept asking what he intended to do, as though childcare did not answer the question. His response brought the two activities together: he would care for the children while she wrote about caring for them.

The dry exchange makes the conditions of writing visible. Unless someone takes over the care, the person who has lived through an experience may have no time to write it down. A book about motherhood that hides the person making that time available risks presenting writing as an achievement of willpower alone.

The arrangement did not instantly dissolve Cusk’s conflict. In the introduction, leaving a child and remaining with a child each have difficulties. The former is not untroubled freedom, the latter not naturally complete belonging. Work and care require negotiation; even a workable division does not allocate feelings equally neatly.

The question about cakes now seems more than a social blunder. Cusk is trying to find an entrance to her old world within a new life, while others may not wish to enter by that route. Their shared identity as mothers has not erased differences or supplied ready-made friends. Outside her former professional surroundings, even picking up a conversation can require learning again.

Her isolation coexists with her own prejudices. She observes other mothers sharply, sometimes seeming reluctant to understand why they value their lives. Readers need not defend every discomfort as insight. Precisely because this is one woman’s account, awkwardness, superiority, and a wish for help can appear together. Removing the unattractive elements might make it less credible.

## Beyond the kitchen, a room in a poem

Literature here does not furnish decorative quotations. Cusk returns to works she has read before with new difficulties in mind. Coleridge’s “Frost at Midnight” becomes an especially moving instance. She notices again that the poem contains a baby and an adult remaining indoors beside it.

Written in the late eighteenth century, the poem begins at night, with others asleep and a father’s thoughts moving from the still room to his own childhood. Having felt confined by city and school, he hopes his child will grow up among lakes and mountains. The room is quiet, but the poem does not stay within it. Memory, wishes, and the seasons enter through his thinking.

For Cusk, feeling confined at home, the poem’s force changes. She knew it already, but accompanying an infant now enables another reading: remaining bodily in one place need not mean the mind can only contract. A child brings attachment and also prompts someone to imagine a future she will not entirely inhabit.

Literature has not prescribed a painkiller. After reading, the baby still needs care and another sleepless night may follow. What the poem briefly loosens is an unduly narrow choice between returning to the formerly free writer and being nothing but a mother. The change she is undergoing can itself become a source of thought, altering how she reads and sees.

This helps explain why the book’s literary excursions are not all dispensable. Readers seeking a straightforward account of childcare may find them circuitous. For this writer, however, reading is one way to understand experience. The poem does not prove that motherhood must eventually bring happiness. It holds together the possibility of confinement and expansion.

Nor should this moment become a tidy ending in an introduction to the book. A reading that changes perspective does not settle every grievance. Cusk preserves instability: a little understanding arrives, and another bout of crying can return her to confusion.

## She need not first become a likable mother

A Life’s Work provoked strong disagreement. Some readers recognized feelings they had been afraid to express; others found its resentment and exaggeration hard to bear. Chinese translator Huang Jianshu specifically reminded readers that the book contains tenderness as well as darkness. Neither should stand for the whole.

That is more precise than simply praising the courage to tell the truth. Truthfulness does not mean recording only the least flattering feelings, nor does it make every judgment correct. Cusk’s strength is her refusal immediately to neutralize a conflict with a reassuring sentence. Irritation can persist, and tenderness can appear somewhere undignified.

The limits of the account remain important. A writer able to publish and negotiate a different division of paid work is not without resources. Her choice to leave some relatives and background outside the frame also means this is not a complete family record. The genuineness of her feelings and the fairness of every portrayal are separate matters.

These limits do not remove the book’s difficult question: after becoming a mother, can a woman still appear as someone who judges, makes mistakes, and does not always please us? If we can only praise her sacrifice or condemn her selfishness, we have two roles rather than much knowledge of a person.

Cusk writes the life within the role. Sometimes she misreads another person; sometimes she finally understands an old poem. She has not stopped loving her child or thinking about her work. The book does not ask us to decide which part is the real woman. It shows her continuing to live among desires that pull against one another, still searching for sentences that can tell us what this is like.
